summary:
Palau decriminalised same-sex conduct in 2014. The Penal Code signed by the President in April 2014 dropped the sodomy offence formerly at section 2803 of Chapter 28, "Sex Crimes", Title 17, which carried up to ten years' imprisonment; Palau's Attorney General confirmed the repeal. No offence against consensual same-sex conduct is currently in force.

Palau's government has a dated record of opposing anti-LGBT violence and discrimination. At its 2011 Universal Periodic Review, Palau accepted recommendations to repeal criminalisation and to combat discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity. In March 2011, Palau was among the 84 countries on whose behalf Colombia delivered a joint statement to the Human Rights Council calling for an end to violence and human-rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity.

No legal gender recognition pathway is available: the sources document no procedure by which a trans person can amend the gender marker on Palau identity or travel documents, so visitors should expect documents to reflect the marker assigned at issuance.

No anti-trans violence is documented in the available record for Palau. The absence of incidents should not be read as a finding of safety. Palau's population is very small and the evidence base correspondingly thin, which gives this assessment greater-than-usual uncertainty.
tangentialFactors:
Palau is a small, US-associated, tourism-dependent economy, and the visitor economy concentrates foreigners into a narrow set of resorts, dive operators and venues where visibility is high and anonymity is low.

Palau's 2011 UPR position was shared with other small states; Nauru accepted recommendations to decriminalise homosexual acts at the same review cycle. Palau's repeal in 2014 lowered the global count of countries criminalising sodomy to 79.

The record is diplomatic and legislative rather than experiential: the sources capture Palau's statements to UN bodies and the text of its Penal Code, but contain no field reporting on how trans visitors are treated by police, hotel staff or immigration officers.
localsOnly:
Residents lived under a sodomy offence of up to ten years' imprisonment until the Penal Code signed in April 2014 removed section 2803 from Title 17. The Attorney General's confirmation is the authoritative statement that the offence is gone.

Palau accepted, at its 2011 Universal Periodic Review, recommendations to repeal criminalisation of same-sex conduct and to combat LGBT discrimination. Those accepted recommendations are the standing basis on which residents can press the government for implementation.

Palau co-sponsored, through Colombia's delivery, the March 2011 joint Human Rights Council statement on behalf of 84 countries calling for an end to violence and violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity. That is the earliest dated record of Palau's stated position in this inventory.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: no source in the inventory describes any legal gender recognition procedure, statutory basis or refusal ground. The finding that no pathway exists rests on the absence of any such record rather than on a cited provision.

Unresolved: the inventory does not state whether the 2014 Penal Code contains offences keyed to gender identity, cross-dressing or so-called indecency, nor whether Palau has anti-discrimination or hate-crime legislation covering gender identity.

Unresolved: nothing is sourced on recognition of same-sex partners or marriages, on bathroom or facilities rules, on access to gender-affirming care, or on whether Palauan entry and visa screening asks questions that could disclose a trans person's status.

Unresolved: there is no sourced record of anti-trans violence in either direction. No incident reports, police statistics or victim accounts appear in the inventory, so the absence of documented cases cannot be treated as evidence that none occur.
